title: PSR-4 Autoloading
learning_outcomes: Explain what psr-4 autoloading contributes to a PHP application.
Apply at least one of these concepts in a small example: namespace prefixes.
Check one edge case and explain how to diagnose unexpected behavior.

content.intro: Composer describes dependencies and maps namespaces to source files. Lockfiles make application installs reproducible; declared constraints and maintenance/security review keep dependency choices intentional. In this lesson, focus on namespace prefixes; then compare it with source directories. Use the example to predict a result before checking it, and record one case where the behavior may differ.
content.why_it_matters: You will use psr-4 autoloading when building readable, testable PHP programs. Its practical value is knowing which rule applies, what result to expect, and how to handle failure or unexpected input.

content_blocks.title: A small PHP example for PSR-4 Autoloading
content_blocks.code:
<?php
$file = tempnam(sys_get_temp_dir(), "php-course-");
if ($file === false) { throw new RuntimeException("Cannot create temp file"); }
file_put_contents($file, "ready\n");
echo trim((string) file_get_contents($file)) . PHP_EOL;
unlink($file);

common_mistakes.why: Updates can overwrite manual changes and make builds irreproducible.
common_mistakes.fix: Declare dependencies in composer.json and regenerate the lock/autoload state using Composer.

common_mistakes.why: Different environments may resolve different dependency versions.
common_mistakes.fix: Commit the lockfile for applications and use the project’s intended install workflow.

common_mistakes.problem: Choosing a package by download count alone.
common_mistakes.why: Popularity does not prove security, maintenance, or version compatibility.
common_mistakes.fix: Review maintenance activity, releases, dependencies, license, and docs.
